style_when: the article explains how a system, process or stack actually works — money flows, supply chains, pipelines, an agent assembly line
prompt: Clean technical isometric cutaway on a weathered concrete plant floor. A rack-mounted task object module sits off-centre, built from brushed steel, graphite anodised aluminium, and safety yellow polymer; a central latching connector feeds three parallel copper contact routes—one dead-ended, one with a stored handle token, one entering a covered 37-position state selector track with interlocking cards. A single directional light rakes from the upper left across the assembly, casting long contact shadows. Deep pine green, slate grey, and safety yellow palette. No text, no logos, no legible lettering. Asymmetric axonometric cutaway with the task object off-centre and generous empty margin.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, watermarks, UI labels, numbers
rationale: The article is a technical architecture explanation of how state is owned between calls; a constructed isometric cutaway can show the task object, handle path, and state matrix as engineered hardware without slipping into generic datacenter photography or plumbing.
subject: a rack-mounted task object module with a 37-position state selector track and latching connector rails
core_thesis: An agent-to-agent hop that stores its state in a task object the protocol owns costs a measured 643 extra lines, six coordination steps, and a 37-state machine with 11 flaws, so the task protocol is worth buying only when work must outlive the call.
core_conflict: Stateless tool-call simplicity versus task-protocol durability: the task keeps the fact between calls but adds a 37-state machine, six coordination steps, and attack surface.
